reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented inspection of a set U of 1,000 parts. F is the set of flagged parts, with |F| = 120, and A is the set of actually defective parts. 90 parts are in both, and 30 defective parts are not flagged, so |A| = 120.

Derivation: true positives are F ∩ A, 90 parts; false positives are F \ A, 120 − 90 = 30; false negatives are A \ F, 30; true negatives lie outside F ∪ A. Precision is |F ∩ A| / |F| = 90 / 120 = 0.75 and recall is |F ∩ A| / |A| = 90 / 120 = 0.75.
Independent check: by inclusion–exclusion, |F ∪ A| = 120 + 120 − 90 = 150, so 1,000 − 150 = 850 parts are true negatives, and 90 + 30 + 30 + 850 = 1,000 accounts for every part exactly once.

Misconception to reject: 'high accuracy means the detector works.' Accuracy is (90 + 850) / 1,000 = 94%, but a detector that flags nothing at all scores (1,000 − 120) / 1,000 = 88% while catching no defects. When defects are rare, accuracy is dominated by the easy negatives.

Change one factor: lower the detector's threshold so it flags 200 parts and catches 110 of the 120 defective ones. Precision falls to 110 / 200 = 0.55 and recall rises to 110 / 120 ≈ 0.917; the threshold trades one kind of error for the other.

Source and limits: scikit-learn's guide to metrics and scoring defines precision as tp / (tp + fp) and recall as tp / (tp + fn): https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html.
